name: ascii
desc: List ASCII idiomatic names and octal/decimal code-point forms
why: Eric Raymond's ASCII reference tool with idiomatic names is a charming old-school curiosity, though shallow.

brief.what_it_is: A command-line tool called ascii that takes a character in almost any notation (a literal character, caret form like ^A, C escape like \n, hex, decimal, octal, binary, ISO/ECMA code, teletype mnemonic, HTML entity name, or slang name) and prints every other known name and code-point form for that character. Run with no arguments it prints a small ASCII chart. Output options -d, -x, -o and -b force the output radix, and -t gives script-friendly output. It is also usable as a quick base converter for 8-bit values.
brief.why_it_exists: Eric S. Raymond wrote it in November 1990 to make it easy to translate between the many ways ASCII characters are named and written, which the homepage says is especially handy for reading cc(1)'s octal 'invalid-character' messages and for serial communications work.
brief.how_it_works: Each argument is tried against every convention the tool knows, and if an argument could mean more than one character, names for all of the candidates are printed. Unrecognized or out-of-range arguments are silently ignored. Prefixes select an interpretation: h, 0x, x or \x for hex; d, 0d or \d for decimal; 0o, o or \o for octal; 0b, b or \b for binary. The man page says comparisons are case-insensitive and dashes map to spaces.

commands_seen.context: Synopsis line from the man page. Shows the options and the optional character-alias argument; it is a usage template, not an example.
Mentioned in the man page text: with no options, ascii behaves like ascii -h, which shows the options summary and a simple ASCII table.

brief.install_notes: Installs with brew install ascii, as the Homebrew scout notes list it. The upstream project distributes a gzipped source tarball (ascii-3.32.tar.gz) and says the code is usually packaged as 'ascii' by distributions. The project repository is at https://gitlab.com/esr/ascii. I did not see any runtime, account, or configuration requirements.
brief.standout: A single small tool that cross-references nearly every naming scheme for a character in one place, including USENET-era hacker slang names, Teletype mnemonics, ISO/ECMA code positions, and HTML/SGML entity names, and can run from any notation as input.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage is dated 01 Mar 2026 and lists version 3.32 with recent changes (hardening flags for packagers, and -d/-o/-x/-b forcing the output radix). The man page says it was last updated 2026-02-17. The project's repository and release history were not fetched, so I did not confirm a last commit date.
brief.caveats: The -s option will not recognize long names, because they cannot be told apart from other parts of a string. Shell metacharacters, especially backslash, must be quoted or stringized in arguments. Unrecognized arguments are silently ignored, so typos produce no error. The man page does not show worked examples. The license is in a COPYING file that I did not open, so I cannot state it. The homepage asks for support via Patreon or SubscribeStar and lists supporters.
quotes: Given any one on the command line, it will try to display all others.
Called with no arguments it displays a handy small ASCII chart.
As a side effect it serves as a handy base-converter for random 8-bit values.
